extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, regulators, researchers interested in automotive emissions and corporate governance
extracted.subtask_description: A comprehensive Wikipedia-style article documenting the Volkswagen TDI emissions scandal: its discovery, technical details (defeat devices), media and public reaction, regulatory and legal responses, recalls, corporate and market consequences, and health/academic studies of impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of defeat devices (EU Regulation 715/2007, Article 5(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 5 (2) of Regulation (EC) No 715/2007 prohibits the use of defeat devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted FAQ: Article 5 (2) of Euro 6 Regulation 715/2007 prohibits the use of defeat devices; this is the legal basis for finding a vehicle non-compliant where software or other design elements circumvent emissions controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'defeat device' (Article 3(10))
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 3(10) defines a defeat device as "any element of design which senses temperature, vehicle speed, engine speed (RPM), transmission gear, manifold vacuum or any other parameter for the purpose of activating, modulating, delaying or deactivating the operation of any part of the emission control system, that reduces the effectiveness of the emission control system under conditions which may reasonably be expected to be encountered in normal vehicle operation and use."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parameters listed (temperature, vehicle speed, RPM, gear, manifold vacuum, or any other parameter) are examples of triggers; the key evaluative point is whether sensing those parameters purposefully reduces emission control effectiveness under normal operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory enforcement under the U.S. Clean Air Act (EPA/DOJ actions)
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. regulators (EPA, CARB, Department of Justice) alleged Clean Air Act violations and issued Notices of Violation, ordered recalls, and filed complaints against Volkswagen, Audi, and Porsche.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory response can include NOVs, mandatory recalls, civil enforcement actions, criminal prosecutions, and large settlements/fines (e.g., multi-billion-dollar US settlement, criminal fines). The page documents examples of such enforcement and outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recall mechanism: voluntary recall versus compulsory recall
rubrics_metrics.description: Volkswagen initially proposed a voluntary recall; Germany's Federal Motor Transport Authority (KBA) ordered a compulsory recall requiring removal of the software and appropriate measures to ensure emissions rules are fulfilled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voluntary recall places onus on individual vehicle owners to seek remedy; compulsory recall requires regulators to mandate fixes for all affected vehicles. The legal/regulatory authority can force a universal remedy if a design element is deemed illegal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for realistic (in-use) emissions testing (PEMS and on-road testing)
rubrics_metrics.description: On-road testing and Portable Emission Measurement Systems (PEMS) revealed elevated NOx emissions in real-world driving compared to laboratory test cycles, exposing discrepancies that lab tests missed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page cites WVU, JRC, and other studies showing that complementary real-world testing (PEMS) is essential to detecting manipulation that targets laboratory cycles; implication: robust regulatory testing should include in-use measurements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate consequences in sustainability/ethical rankings
rubrics_metrics.description: S&P Dow Jones Indices and RobecoSAM delisted Volkswagen AG from the Dow Jones Sustainability indexes, citing social and ethical reasons; Volkswagen lost its Industry Group Leader status in 'Automobiles & Components.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corporate behavior on ethics and social responsibility can be grounds for removal from sustainability indices and loss of related recognitions; such delisting is a reputational and market signal beyond legal penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rescinding environmental awards upon evidence of manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Green Car Journal rescinded its 'Green Car of the Year' awards for models previously recognized for environmental performance after the scandal emerged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Awards tied to environmental performance rely on truthful evidence; discovery of deception (e.g., emissions cheating) can justify revocation of honors and public retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies and settlements as enforcement outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal and regulatory resolutions include buybacks, compensation for owners, recall remedies (software/hardware fixes), civil settlements, fines, and criminal fines (examples: record multi-billion-dollar settlements and fines documented).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcement instruments vary by jurisdiction and case: outcomes may include consumer compensation, mandated technical fixes, corporate fines, criminal penalties, and long-term monitoring or buyback programs; the page lists numerous jurisdiction-specific examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual liability and criminal prosecution of executives
rubrics_metrics.description: Executives and engineers were investigated, charged, indicted, or sentenced in connection with the emissions-cheating scheme (e.g., six executives charged, ex-CEO charged with fraud, engineers pleading guilty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory and criminal investigations can extend to individuals within a corporation; evidence of intentional deception can produce criminal charges and prison sentences beyond corporate fines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical detection by independent researchers and code analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent academic and industry researchers (WVU study, portable emissions equipment, code analysis) played a central role in discovering the cheating, including finding computer code used to cheat tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page highlights that independent in-use testing and analysis of vehicle software/code can uncover manipulative elements not detected by manufacturer-submitted data; transparency and independent verification are implied standards for credible compliance testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public health impact assessment of excess emissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Academic studies estimated the public health consequences of excess NOx emissions from the defeat-device-equipped fleet, e.g., integrated over the sales period producing an estimate of 59 (95% CI: 10 to 150) early deaths in the US.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimating health impacts requires integrating emissions over time and applying epidemiological models; results have uncertainty (confidence intervals) and are used to quantify societal harm in regulatory, legal, and public discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory scope and international variation in response
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses and findings varied by jurisdiction (EPA/CARB in the US, KBA in Germany, EU regulations), with different legal frameworks, recall decisions, and timelines (e.g., Germany ordered compulsory recall; the US pursued recall and large settlements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulators' statutory powers and procedural choices differ across countries; compliance assessments and remedies depend on local laws and the interpretation of regulations such as the EU's defeat-device prohibition or the US Clean Air Act.
